मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र के पूर्वानुमान के मुताबिक, 7 नवंबर को सुबह कोहरा छाया रहेगा, जबकि मौसम शुष्क रहेगा. 8 नवंबर को सुबह में कुहासा और दिन में आंशिक बादल छाए रह सकते हैं. 9 नवंबर को रांची में सुबह कोहरा और बादल रहने का अनुमान है. वहीं, राज्य के उत्तर-पूर्वी और दक्षिण-पूर्वी हिस्सों में कहीं-कहीं हल्की बारिश या मेघ गर्जन हो सकता है.
10 नवंबर को रांची समेत कई जिलों में सुबह कोहरा और बादल छाए रहेंगे. इस दौरान पश्चिमी सिंहभूम, पूर्वी सिंहभूम, सरायकेला, देवघर, जामताड़ा, दुमका, गोड्डा, साहिबगंज और पाकुड़ में बारिश की संभावना है.

13 नवंबर से साफ होगा मौसम, फिर बढ़ेगा तापमान
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, 12 नवंबर को राज्य के कई हिस्सों में आंशिक बादल छाए रह सकते हैं. इसके बाद 13 नवंबर से मौसम साफ रहने की उम्मीद है. अगले तीन दिनों में तापमान गिरने के बाद दो दिनों के दौरान न्यूनतम तापमान में 2 से 4 डिग्री सेल्सियस की बढ़ोतरी हो सकती है. फिलहाल 7 से 11 नवंबर तक राज्य के किसी भी जिले के लिए मौसम विभाग ने कोई विशेष चेतावनी जारी नहीं की है.

UP Weather Today: बदलने लगा लखनऊ का मिजाज, हवा में नमी बढ़ने से महसूस हुई हल्की ठंड
लखनऊ में मौसम में बदलाव जारी है, न्यूनतम तापमान 17.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस पहुंचा और हवा में नमी बढ़ी है। शहर ...और पढ़ें

लखनऊ का न्यूनतम तापमान 17.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस, नमी में वृद्धि।
शहर का वायु गुणवत्ता सूचकांक (AQI) 301, 'बहुत खराब' श्रेणी में।
हरदोई 14.0 डिग्री सेल्सियस के साथ प्रदेश का सबसे ठंडा जिला।
जागरण संवाददाता, लखनऊ। मौसम में बदलाव जारी है। आने वाले सात दिनों में हवा में नमी बढ़ेगी और न्यूनतम तापमान में तीन-चार फीसदी गिरावट देखने को मिल सकती है।इससे सुबह और शाम हल्की ठंड का एहसास होगा। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, राजधानी लखनऊ में शुक्रवार का अधिकतम तापमान 30.9 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया है।
वहीं, न्यूनतम तापमान 17.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा है। हवा में अधिकतम नमी 94 प्रतिशत और न्यूनतम नमी 44 प्रतिशत दर्ज की गई। वहीं, हवा की गुणवत्ता लगातार खराब हो रही है। शुक्रवार को एक्यूआइ का स्तर 301 पहुंच गया।
प्रादेशिक मौसम केंद्र के मुताबिक, प्रदेश के कई हिस्सों में पिछले दो दिनों से हल्का कोहरा पड़ना शुरू हो गया है। साथ ही, धुंध भी छा रही है। वहीं, शुक्रवार को भी हरदोई सबसे ठंडा जिला रहा। वहां न्यूनतम तापमान सामान्य से 2.9 डिग्री सेल्सियस गिरकर 14.0 डिग्री सेल्सियस पहुंच चुका है। इसके अलावा मुजफ्फरनगर में भी न्यूनतम तापमान 14.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस रिकार्ड किया गया।
पूर्वी और पश्चिमी उत्तर प्रदेश के दोनों भागों में आगामी 12 नवंबर तक मौसम के पूरी तरह सामान्य रहने की संभावना जताई गई है। पूरे राज्य में मौसम सामान्य बना हुआ है। आने वाले सात दिनों में भी किसी बड़े उलटफेर की संभावना नहीं है। अगले सात दिनों तक प्रदेश में कई जिलों में हल्का कोहरा छा सकता और हल्की धुंध देखने को मिल सकती है।

राजधानी में 300 पार हुआ एक्यूआइ
शुक्रवार को शहर की गुणवत्ता काफी खराब रही। तालकटोरा में शाम छह बजे एक्यूआइ का स्तर 301 (बहुत खराब) पहुंच गया। वहीं, अलीगंज में एक्यूआइ 2570 रहा। बीआर अंबेडकर विश्वविद्यालय के क्षेत्र में एक्यूआइ 143 और लालबाग में एक्यूआइ 213 रहा। वहीं, कुकरैल की हवा खराब होती जा रही है।वहां शुक्रवार को एक्यूआइ 165 और गोमतीनगर में एक्यूआइ 114 रहा।

full_text:
रायपुर : छत्तीसगढ़ में बारिश की गतिविधियां कमजोर पड़ने के साथ ही मौसम ने करवट लेना शुरू कर दिया है। प्रदेश में अब आसमान साफ होने लगा है और ठंडी हवाओं के कारण सुबह तथा रात के समय हल्की सर्दी का एहसास होने लगा है। बंगाल की खाड़ी में बने चक्रवाती तूफान का असर कमजोर होने के बाद प्रदेश में शुष्क मौसम की स्थिति बन रही है।मौसम विभाग ने आगामी दिनों को लेकर पूर्वानुमान जारी किया है। इसके मुताबिक अगले तीन दिनों में प्रदेश के न्यूनतम तापमान में 1 से 3 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक गिरावट आ सकती है। इसके बाद तापमान में किसी बड़े बदलाव के आसार नहीं हैं। ऐसे में नवंबर के शुरुआती दिनों के साथ ही छत्तीसगढ़ में सर्दी का असर धीरे-धीरे बढ़ने की संभावना है।
अगले तीन दिनों में और बढ़ेगी ठंड
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, 7 नवंबर से प्रदेश के अधिकांश हिस्सों में मौसम शुष्क रहने का अनुमान है। बारिश की गतिविधियां कम होने और आसमान साफ रहने के कारण रात के तापमान में गिरावट दर्ज की जा सकती है।अगले तीन दिनों के दौरान न्यूनतम तापमान 1 से 3 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक नीचे जा सकता है। इसका सबसे ज्यादा असर सुबह और देर रात के मौसम में महसूस होगा। हालांकि, इसके बाद न्यूनतम तापमान में विशेष बदलाव होने की संभावना नहीं जताई गई है।
अंबिकापुर में सबसे ठंडी रही रात, न्यूनतम तापमान 14.3 डिग्री
पिछले 24 घंटों के मौसम संबंधी आंकड़ों में अंबिकापुर प्रदेश का सबसे ठंडा इलाका रहा। यहां न्यूनतम तापमान 14.3 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया।दूसरी ओर, राजधानी रायपुर और माना में अधिकतम तापमान 31.1 डिग्री सेल्सियस रिकॉर्ड किया गया। यह प्रदेश में सबसे अधिक रहा। इससे साफ है कि प्रदेश के उत्तरी और मैदानी इलाकों के तापमान में अंतर बना हुआ है।
कोहकामेटा में हुई सबसे अधिक बारिश
प्रदेश में अब बारिश का प्रभाव काफी कम हो गया है। पिछले 24 घंटों के दौरान छत्तीसगढ़ के एक-दो स्थानों पर हल्की से मध्यम बारिश दर्ज की गई। इस दौरान कोहकामेटा में सबसे अधिक 4 सेंटीमीटर वर्षा रिकॉर्ड की गई।मौसम विभाग का अनुमान है कि आने वाले दिनों में बारिश की गतिविधियां और कमजोर होंगी। इसके साथ ही रात के तापमान में गिरावट का सिलसिला जारी रह सकता है।
रायपुर में आसमान रहेगा साफ, 19 डिग्री तक पहुंच सकता है पारा
राजधानी रायपुर में 7 नवंबर को मौसम मुख्य रूप से साफ रहने का अनुमान है। यहां अधिकतम तापमान करीब 31 डिग्री सेल्सियस और न्यूनतम तापमान लगभग 19 डिग्री सेल्सियस रह सकता है।दिन के समय लोगों को गर्मी से ज्यादा परेशानी होने की संभावना नहीं है, लेकिन सुबह और रात के समय हल्की ठंड महसूस होगी। आने वाले दिनों में न्यूनतम तापमान में गिरावट के चलते राजधानी में सर्दी का असर और बढ़ सकता है।
तेलंगाना और आंध्र प्रदेश के ऊपर बना चक्रवाती परिसंचरण
मौसम विभाग के मुताबिक पूर्वी तेलंगाना और उससे लगे तटीय आंध्र प्रदेश के ऊपर ऊपरी वायु में चक्रवाती परिसंचरण सक्रिय है। यह मौसमी सिस्टम समुद्र तल से करीब 4.5 किलोमीटर की ऊंचाई पर स्थित है।हालांकि, इसके कारण छत्तीसगढ़ के मौसम में फिलहाल किसी बड़े बदलाव की संभावना नहीं जताई गई है। प्रदेश में अगले कुछ दिनों तक शुष्क मौसम बने रहने का अनुमान है।
नवंबर में धीरे-धीरे बढ़ेगा सर्दी का असर
छत्तीसगढ़ में बारिश का दौर समाप्त होने के बाद अब मौसम सर्दियों की ओर बढ़ रहा है। न्यूनतम तापमान में संभावित गिरावट से प्रदेश के कई जिलों में सुबह और रात की ठंडक बढ़ेगी।फिलहाल मौसम विभाग ने अगले तीन दिनों में तापमान 1 से 3 डिग्री तक गिरने का अनुमान जताया है। इसके बाद मौसम में स्थिरता रह सकती है। ऐसे में आने वाले दिनों में लोगों को सुबह और देर रात हल्की गर्माहट वाले कपड़ों की जरूरत महसूस होने लगेगी।

As temperatures rise across Nigeria, extreme heat can do more than cause discomfort. From dehydration and disrupted sleep to heat exhaustion and potentially life-threatening heatstroke, understanding how the body responds to high temperatures can help people recognise the warning signs and protect their health.

The increasingly extreme heat not only threatens food production but also endangers the health and safety of millions of workers who have long been overlooked.
07 Nov 2026 12:00 WIB · Lingkungan
So far, the impact of climate change in Indonesia has often been measured in terms of production figures—how many hectares of rice fields have failed, how many tons of rice have been lost, how many days fishermen have been unable to go to sea, and the trillions of rupiah in economic losses incurred. However, there is a loss that is much closer to human life and has been overlooked in these calculations: the human body working under extreme heat.
Farmers spending hours tilling the fields, fishermen braving the sun on the open sea, and outdoor workers facing risks of dehydration, fatigue, sleep disturbances, anxiety, and even life-threatening illnesses are no longer a distant future threat.
Extreme heat has become a part of life for communities across various regions in Indonesia. If the latest climate change projections hold true, what is currently being experienced may just be the beginning.
A study led by Philipp Aglas-Leitner of Freie Universität Berlin and published in the journal Nature Communications on November 5, 2026, warns that future heat waves could far exceed the extreme events humans have experienced in recent years.
The study, "Recent Extreme Heatwaves Are No Match for Future Events," analyzed 22 exceptional heatwaves that occurred between 2010 and 2023 in various regions of the world, including Europe, Australia, China, India and Pakistan, North Africa and the Middle East, and South America. Nine events from 2015 to 2023 were examined in more depth.
Unlike studies that merely compare temperature records, this research analyzes multiple characteristics simultaneously, including duration, heat accumulation, average and maximum severity, as well as the extent of the affected areas. The researchers utilized data from Berkeley Earth and ERA5, along with climate model projections from CMIP5 and CMIP6 for the period from 2020 to 2100 under various emission scenarios.
"Most heatwaves in the future will exceed the extraordinary events we have experienced recently," said Philipp Aglas-Leitner, the lead author of the study. "The events currently being observed will be surpassed by a significant margin, especially towards the end of the 21st century."
The findings of this study are indeed concerning. Most projections indicate that future heatwaves will last longer, cover broader areas, be more severe, and result in significantly higher heat accumulation compared to extreme events previously observed.
Between 2060 and 2099, most models for many of the studied regions project at least one extraordinary heatwave each year. In Europe, heatwaves could last for several months, affecting large parts of the continent.
Researchers also caution that even ambitious emission reductions cannot completely shield humanity from extreme heat waves. Therefore, emission cuts must be accompanied by serious adaptation efforts.
Although Indonesia was not specifically analyzed in the study, its warnings are relevant for tropical countries with millions of residents working outdoors. Moreover, signs of increasing heat risk are already evident in Indonesia.
The LaporIklim study report with the People's Coalition for Food Sovereignty (KRKP), on Invisible Heat (2026), shows how climate change has affected human health.
This study used a rapid health and climate survey of 300 farmers and fishermen in Indramayu Regency, West Java, and Kupang City and Regency, East Nusa Tenggara. The results were combined with meteorological trend analysis from the Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG).
A total of 78.3 percent of respondents reported experiencing severe muscle cramps, intense dizziness, or near-fainting while working. Additionally, 91 percent indicated that they sometimes have to stop working due to heat. Furthermore, 80.3 percent reported having difficulty sleeping because of nighttime heat.
In Indramayu, daytime temperatures have risen by an average of 0.28 degrees Celsius per decade since 1991, while nighttime temperatures have increased by 0.41 degrees Celsius. In Kupang, the increase in daytime temperatures has reached 0.4 degrees Celsius per decade, with nighttime temperatures rising by 0.33 degrees Celsius.
The rise in nighttime temperatures warrants special attention. The human body needs time to recover after being exposed to heat throughout the day. When nights remain warm, the body's opportunity to release heat and rest diminishes, leading to a cumulative effect of fatigue day after day.
Adaptation strategies need to shift from a production-centered approach to protecting the people who produce food.
This threat goes beyond mere workplace comfort. In Indramayu, 47 percent of fishermen reported having nearly fainted while at sea. Additionally, 94.7 percent of fishermen in the region have directly experienced extreme weather events while out on the water.
This means that climate change has now entered the realm of occupational safety. Farmers and fishermen are not only facing the threats of crop failure, declining catches, or asset damage due to extreme weather. They are also risking their health and safety to maintain food production.
The issue is that Indonesia's climate adaptation policies are still largely production-oriented. For instance, the success of agricultural adaptation is often measured by crop productivity, the area of protected land, or the volume of production that has been maintained. In fisheries, metrics include catch yields and the number of days spent at sea.
While these measures are important, they are not sufficient. Food production may be maintained, but at an increasingly high cost to the health of those who produce it.
Another dimension that has been overlooked is mental health. A survey by LaporIklim found that 39 percent of respondents often feel irritable. Additionally, 31.7 percent frequently or very often experience sleep difficulties due to anxiety. Among fishermen in Indramayu, the anxiety rate reaches 65.3 percent.
This anxiety is closely tied to the uncertainties of their lives. Farmers are facing increasingly unpredictable planting seasons and the threat of crop failure. Fishermen are confronted with extreme weather that endangers their safety and creates uncertainty about their income.
Extreme heat is not an isolated threat; it intertwines with economic pressures, food insecurity, and social vulnerabilities. Sleep disturbances and anxiety exacerbate physical fatigue, while economic strain makes it increasingly difficult for workers to take breaks or stop working.
A cycle of vulnerability has emerged: as the body becomes increasingly fatigued, the risk of health issues and accidents rises. However, when income is uncertain, workers feel compelled to continue working even when their physical condition does not allow it.
Adaptation that merely requires individuals to change their behavior without improving working conditions ultimately shifts the burden of the climate crisis onto those who have contributed the least to its causes.
Research findings from Aglas-Leitner and the LaporIklim study convey complementary messages. Future heatwaves are likely to far exceed current human experiences. Meanwhile, the existing heat conditions have already caused physical and mental health issues for Indonesia's food workers. Therefore, adaptation strategies must shift from a production-centered approach to one that prioritizes the protection of the individuals who produce food.
There are six policy agendas that need to be strengthened. First, developing a health system that can adapt to heat, including the capacity of healthcare facilities to recognize and address heat-related illnesses. Second, expanding social protection for farmers and fishermen so they can cease work during unsafe conditions without losing their entire income.
Third, develop a Heat Safety Guideline specifically for farmers and fishermen that outlines work hours, rest periods, access to drinking water, shelter locations, and procedures for halting activities when heat risks reach dangerous levels. Fourth, strengthen community-based adaptation by integrating local knowledge with meteorological information.
Fifth, integrate heat risks into regional development planning through coordination among the health, agriculture, fisheries, labor, and disaster management sectors. Sixth, pay special attention to mental health and vulnerable families, including women, children, and the elderly.
Indonesia has a significant interest in addressing this threat. As a tropical country with millions of farmers and fishermen relying on outdoor work, rising temperatures are not merely a matter of comfort. This issue pertains to workplace safety, public health, livelihood sustainability, and food security.
There is a paradox that needs to be addressed: how can we discuss food security when the health of those who produce food is increasingly at risk?
The success of climate adaptation should not be measured solely by the number of hectares of productive rice fields, the tons of fish caught, or the extent of economic losses mitigated. Equally important metrics include the number of people protected and the diseases that can be prevented.
We must not succeed in maintaining food production, but sacrifice the health and safety of the people who produce it.

"If we have more summers like the last two, we'll be struggling as a nation to produce enough Christmas trees."
Andrew Ingram owns The Tree Barn in Christmas Common, Oxfordshire, which is home to about 120,000 trees.
But this year's hot summer and drought has reduced that total by more than a thousand.
"It's been an extraordinary year," he said. "We planted in perfect conditions in March and then it didn't rain for 12 weeks until the first week of June.
"Then after that it didn't rain until September, it's very depressing."
Russell Parkins, chair of the British Christmas Tree Association, agreed that growers across the country had faced a "tough year".
He said his organisation was working on "ongoing research to help ensure British-grown Christmas trees continue to thrive in a changing climate".
The full impact of the drought is unlikely to be felt immediately, with the biggest consequences potentially coming in years to come.
Some Christmas trees can take up to nine years to reach six feet tall, meaning the loss of young saplings could affect production well into the next decade.
"A transplant we put in will be around a year old and it's replacing a tree that is three to four years old so that's affecting production and could lead to shortages in the future," said Ingram.
"It means we have to walk the rows, pull out the dead trees, replace them by hand…it's a laborious job, a time consuming job and an expensive job."
"We tend to plant in the spring but that's becoming a more dangerous time to plant," Ingram said.
"It would be better to plant in Autumn because that allows the tree to get established and routed in through the winter."
He said there were also concerns that warmer temperatures this winter could mean less frosts.
Frosts help to keep Christmas trees in a dormant state, helping them to hold onto their needles for longer once they've entered our homes for the festive period.
"I think there's a real danger we'll see more trees losing their needles this year," Ingram said.
"We're going to have to figure out ways to carry on growing even if the weather turns against us."

Pagasa Visayas projects Cebu’s heat index could reach an extreme danger level of 52°C as El Niño intensifies the upcoming hot and dry season.
The projected heat index would surpass Cebu’s previous record high of 51°C recorded during a weaker El Niño episode in 2018.
Pagasa Visayas Chief Al Quiblat advised residents to limit direct sun exposure to under 20 minutes to prevent heat-related illnesses like stroke.
CEBU could face extreme heat in the coming months, with the apparent temperature potentially reaching 52 degrees Celsius as El Niño intensifies the effects of the approaching hot and dry season.
The projected heat index could exceed the province’s previous high of 51 degrees Celsius, raising concerns over increased exposure to dangerous conditions as temperatures climb toward summer.
Al Quiblat, chief of the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) Visayas, said the combined influence of El Niño and the country’s hot and dry season, which typically runs from March to May, could produce more pronounced heating.
Historical highs
Pagasa projects heat index readings ranging from 41 to 52 degrees Celsius, although actual conditions will depend on prevailing temperatures and humidity.
“If you combine El Niño with our hot and dry season, its impact will be more pronounced,” Quiblat said.
The projected maximum could surpass Cebu’s previous recorded heat index of 51 degrees Celsius in 2018, when the province experienced a weaker El Niño episode.
Quiblat also pointed to the 2010 El Niño as an example of how the weather phenomenon can drive temperatures beyond their usual levels.
On May 10, 2010, Cebu recorded an air temperature of 37 degrees Celsius — four degrees higher than the month’s average maximum of 33 degrees — which translated to a heat index of 49 degrees Celsius when combined with relative humidity.
Differing weather systems
While these historical records indicate the possible intensity of the current conditions, Quiblat cautioned that El Niño episodes do not produce identical weather patterns.
The agency’s latest projection places the possible heat index as high as 52 degrees Celsius, which would break the previous 51-degree record.
Even the arrival of the northeast monsoon, or Amihan, may not be enough to keep Cebu’s temperatures within their usual range.
Quiblat explained that Amihan and El Niño operate through different weather systems, noting that while the northeast monsoon generally brings cooler winds from mainland Asia, it does not cancel out the warming influence of El Niño.
For November and December, Pagasa expects temperatures to be around 0.5 to 1 degree Celsius above normal.
With Cebu’s average maximum temperature during these months at approximately 31 degrees Celsius, daytime readings could approach 32 degrees.
This means residents may still feel the cooler winds associated with Amihan while experiencing temperatures warmer than what is normally expected for the season.
Heat index factors
The risk from rising temperatures is particularly pronounced during the middle of the day, when air temperatures generally reach their highest levels.
Quiblat said temperatures typically begin increasing at around 10 a.m. before peaking between 1 p.m. and 3 p.m., although heat index readings may reach their highest levels anytime within this window depending on the air temperature and relative humidity.
Pagasa Mactan recorded heat index readings ranging from 38 to 39 degrees Celsius during the week leading up to Sunday, Nov. 8.
The heat index measures how hot conditions feel to the human body by factoring in both actual air temperature and relative humidity; as moisture in the air increases, sweat evaporates more slowly, making it harder for the body to regulate its temperature.
“When relative humidity is high and air temperature is high, the heat index also rises,” he said.
Safety precautions

The US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) has issued an alert notifying consumers across America that 3.6 million ladders are being recalled because they could unexpectedly retract due to faulty locks. According to reports, warning comes after a number of people sustained broken bones, brain damage and other injuries.
US CPSC has published a recall notice warning consumers that approximately 3,662,000 (3.6 million) ladders made by Little Giant Ladder Systems were being recalled after the company received several reports of the ladders unexpectedly retracting, causing serious injuries to users. As per CPSC's warning to buyers: "Ladders can suddenly retract if the Rapid Locks are not fully engaged, posing a fall hazard to consumers."
The faulty ladders have been sold on Lowes, Amazon, Costco, LittleGiantLadders and other websites. As per the consumer body, the 3.6 million-plus ladders included in this recall were sold nationally between December 2015 and October 2026. The ladders sold are priced anywhere from around $100 to around $1,000.
The CPSC's notice says that the Rapid Locks are black or orange components on the ladders’ legs, designed to be inserted to adjust the ladders’ height.
When the Rapid Locks don’t work as intended, the ladders can suddenly retract, causing the user to fall and sustain serious injuries. Little Giant has also published its own recall notice, in which the ladder manufacturer warns of the same hazard.
What US CPSC 'red notice' says
"Consumers should stop using the recalled ladders immediately until they review the information at
http://www.littlegiantladders.com/pages/recalls or via the QR code on the ladder and contact Little Giant for a repair kit containing warning labels and instructions. The additional instructions and labels, which should be affixed to the ladder, advise consumers to verify that their Rapid Locks are properly engaged before every use and to maintain their locks with lubrication. Consumers who follow the provided instructions and have a Rapid Lock that does not function properly after the application of lubrication should contact Little Giant for evaluation. If a lock does not function properly after this evaluation, the company will offer the choice of a replacement ladder of the same or equivalent model or a refund ranging from a depreciated value determined by date of purchase up to full purchase price for ladders purchased within the past 12 months," said the USCPC on its page.
Which ladder models are being recalled
The CPSC says the following models of Little Giant ladders are being recalled: Adjustable Fortress 2.0, Conquest 2.0, Dark Horse 2.0, Epic, King Kombo XT, Leveler, MegaLite, MegaLite+, Multi, Quantum and Vector.

full_text:
Data centres have become so politically toxic that they've managed to bind together the Greens and One Nation.
The two ideological opposites stood side by side at a community rally in Mannum last weekend, speaking out against a Melbourne developer's bid for a hyper-scale data centre in Tungkillo, roughly 40km east of Adelaide, over concerns about the environment, energy and water use.
The Liberal Party was there too, demanding that locals who are fiercely opposed get a genuine say. Mid Murray Council Mayor Simone Bailey, who ran for Labor at the March state election, told the ABC it was "really hard to understand the benefits" of the proposal.
Popular independent federal MP Rebekha Sharkie is also against it, posting on Facebook that "Data Centres do NOT belong on prime agricultural land".
The broad coalition that's forming in Tungkillo comes with the backdrop of the US midterms, where Americans used their ballots as a sledgehammer against pro-data centre proposals and politicians.
Labor in SA should be on red alert.
No data centres for the sake of data centres, premier says
The bulk of the anger in Mannum over the weekend was directed at Quantum DC, a company that has had — to put it mildly — a few hiccups with its community consultation process.
But Labor copped plenty of criticism as well, accused by both Greens MLC Robert Simms and One Nation's Carlos Quaremba of "rolling out the red carpet" for data centres.
The government has reason to dispute that characterisation.
It has drafted new laws proposing tougher energy and water requirements on the computing facilities, with Premier Peter Malinauskas declaring "if they're not in our interests, they're not happening".
The premier appears to have taken plenty of lessons from the US, criticising their "let it rip" approach.
"They have let data centres be built next to residential homes, they have let data centres be built without any reference to new generation coming on board, we've seen blackouts, we've seen price increases, it's madness," he said.
"If it's going to happen in Australia, it cannot happen like that."
Quantum DC is also yet to lodge its planning application for Tungkillo, with the government saying it doesn't want to "pre-judge" the project.
"I don't even know who these people are, like they haven't even applied," Mr Malinauskas said of the Tungkillo proposal.
"And it's causing an awful amount of community anxiety over a process that no one's ever started formally.
"That doesn't represent the sort of way we want to go about engaging with this."
Mr Malinauskas said he wanted to see a "proper regulatory and legislative environment" that allows his government to "stop data centres from happening unless they comply with our standards".
At the same time, however, the premier and his state development minister, Chris Picton, seem to be the only state politicians who this year have offered anything resembling positive commentary about data centres.
The political wisdom of standing alongside Firmus co-founder Oliver Curtis in June to spruik new AI development in SA is quite easy to question in hindsight, particularly given the spectacular collapse of Firmus' IPO four months later.
Not to mention the government's data centre strategy has plenty of verbs in it like "accelerate" and "streamline" to send a chill down the spine of data centre opponents.
"We are proactively engaging global and domestic AI companies and data centre developers to land major investments, build capability, and create high-value jobs for South Australians," the strategy states.
These are all elements that, fairly or unfairly, could come back to haunt Labor should more unpopular AI proposals lob in other marginal seats.
Because currently, there appears to be far more votes to be won leaning into concerns about data centres than courting their arrival.
Rigorous process or concerning gap?
The government's messaging on Tungkillo has also been curious.
On Saturday, Planning Minister Nick Champion spoke to the media to provide some reassurance to the Mannum community, noting the government controlled the planning pathway for the Tungkillo data centre.
"Whatever the pathway, the process is rigorous," he told reporters.
"There is a very rigorous test on power, they cannot jeopardise our grid, they cannot jeopardise the stability or the power capacity of our grid, they have to pass a test on water, and they have to pass rigorous tests in the planning system."
Yet by the time we got to Thursday, the premier was talking about the urgent need for law reform.
"At the moment, data centres can apply for development applications and the like and we don't necessarily have the controls that we desire to be able to ensure that they do bring their own energy, that they do comply with environmental standards," he said.
"We need to be able to restrict these things from happening unless they do it in circumstances that is in the state's interests."
Labor will soon need to pass its data centre legislation through the upper house of parliament, where it does not hold a majority.
Instead, they will need to negotiate with their political opponents who are leaning into data centre angst.
Don't be surprised to see that Greens and One Nation alliance pop up again.
